patterns.name: inna — the certainty opener
patterns.what: إِنَّ starts a sentence with force: 'indeed / truly'. It's everywhere in the Quran. Practical rule: after إِنَّ the noun takes -a (accusative): إِنَّ اللهَ، إِنَّ الإِنسَانَ. With pronouns it fuses: إِنَّهُ (indeed he), إِنَّا (indeed we), إِنَّكَ (indeed you).

examples.en: Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
Indeed mankind is in loss. (103:2)
Indeed We gave you al-Kawthar. (108:1)

test.prompt: '___ Allah is with the patient.' — write the opener

patterns.name: alladhina — 'those who'
patterns.what: الَّذِي (who, m.), الَّتِي (who, f.), الَّذِينَ (those who) glue a description onto a noun. The Quran's most famous phrase: الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا 'those who believe'. Hear الذين and expect a description of a group to follow.

examples.en: Those who believe and do righteous deeds. (103:3)
The path of those You have blessed. (1:7)

examples.ar: ذَٰلِكَ الْكِتَابُ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ هُدًى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ
examples.en: …a guidance for those mindful of Allah. (2:2)

test.prompt: Complete the famous phrase: الَّذِينَ ___ (they believed)

patterns.name: idafa — possession by pairing
patterns.what: Arabic says 'the Lord of the worlds' by just putting two nouns together: رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ. No word for 'of'! First noun never takes ال; the second one usually does. You already know: يَوْمِ الدِّينِ (Day of Judgment), بَيْتِ اللهِ (house of Allah).

examples.en: Lord of the worlds. (1:2)
Master of the Day of Judgment. (1:4)
the people of the house

test.prompt: 'the Day of Judgment' (1:4, two words after مالك)

patterns.name: attached pronouns — my, your, his, their
patterns.what: Arabic attaches its pronouns to the END of words: ـِي my (رَبِّي my Lord), ـكَ your (رَبُّكَ your Lord), ـهُ his/him (لَهُ to him), ـهُمْ their/them (عَلَيْهِمْ upon them), ـنَا our/us (اهْدِنَا guide us). Master these five endings and huge amounts of Quran unlock.

examples.en: So pray to YOUR Lord. (108:2)
Guide US to the straight path. (1:6)
You have blessed THEM. (1:7)

patterns.name: past vs present — the two verb shapes
patterns.what: Past: the root alone — قَالَ he said, خَلَقَ he created, عَلِمَ he knew. Present: add يَـ for 'he' — يَقُولُ he says, يَخْلُقُ he creates, يَعْلَمُ he knows. For 'they' in the past add ـُوا: قَالُوا they said, آمَنُوا they believed. Recognize these two shapes and you can tell WHEN everything happens.

examples.en: your Lord SAID / those who SAY
He CREATED man. (96:2)
they BELIEVED and they DID (103:3)

patterns.name: who's doing it — we vs they
patterns.what: The prefix says WHO, and the tail ـونَ says THEY. نَحْنُ (we): prefix نَـ — the same ن that starts نَحْنُ — and NO tail: نَقُولُ we say, سَنَقُولُ we will say. هُمْ (they): prefix يَـ PLUS the tail ـونَ: يَقُولُونَ they say, سَيَقُولُونَ they will say. In the past the job moves to the ending: we = ـنَا (قُلْنَا we said), they = ـُوا (قَالُوا they said). One rule saves you every time: the ـونَ tail belongs to the crowd — 'we' never wears it.

examples.en: You alone WE worship, You alone WE ask for help (1:5) — نَـ with no tail
THEY say with their mouths (3:167) — يَـ … ـونَ
and when WE said to the angels (2:34) — past 'we' = ـنَا

test.prompt: 'we will say' (سَ + قال — remember: no tail!)

patterns.name: the four ways to say 'not'
patterns.what: لَا + present = doesn't/don't (لَا يَعْلَمُونَ they don't know). مَا + past = didn't (مَا كَانَ he was not). لَمْ + short present = didn't, emphatic (لَمْ يَلِدْ He did not beget). لَنْ + present = will never (لَن تَفْعَلُوا you will never do). When you hear any of these, the sentence flips negative.

examples.en: He did not beget nor was He born. (112:3)
There is no doubt in it. (2:2)
The Day when wealth will not benefit. (26:88)

test.prompt: Which particle negates the PAST with a normal verb? ('he did not...')

patterns.name: the connectors — and, so, then
patterns.what: وَ = and (glued to the next word: وَعَمِلُوا 'and they did'). فَـ = so/then, immediate result (فَصَلِّ 'so pray'). ثُمَّ = then, after a while. Recitation flows on these three — hearing them tells you how ideas link.

examples.en: SO pray to your Lord AND sacrifice. (108:2)
they believed AND did righteous deeds. (103:3)
THEN I drink coffee. (your story!)

patterns.name: preposition + pronoun fusions
patterns.what: Prepositions fuse with pronouns constantly: لِـ+هُ = لَهُ (to him/His), فِي+هِ = فِيهِ (in it), مِنْ+هُ = مِنْهُ (from it), بِـ+هِ = بِهِ (by it), عَلَى+هِ = عَلَيْهِ (upon him), لَـ+هُمْ = لَهُمْ (for them). These tiny fused words carry the Quran's sentences — learn to hear them as units.

examples.en: no doubt IN IT. (2:2)
and there is none comparable TO HIM. (112:4)
FOR THEM is a great reward.

patterns.name: عِندَ — having, and not having
patterns.what: Arabic has no verb 'to have'. It says "at me" — عِندِي بَيْتٌ, literally 'at me is a house'. The pronoun sticks on the end: عِندِي (I have), عِندَكَ (you have), عِندَهُ (he has), عِندَنا (we have), عِندَكُمْ (you all have). To say you DON'T have it, put مَا or لَيْسَ in front: مَا عِندِي and لَيْسَ عِندِي both mean 'I don't have' — لَيْسَ is the more formal one. From the class of 30 Aug.

examples.en: I have a big cupboard.
Do you have a lift?
I don't have time.

test.prompt: 'Do you have a lift?' (asking a household)

patterns.name: the dual — how to make “exactly two”
patterns.what:
English has one and many. Arabic has one, TWO, and many — and the two is an ENDING, not a word. You never say the number.

MAKING IT, in one step: add ـَانِ to the singular. خَال → خَالَانِ (two uncles), كِتَاب → كِتَابَانِ (two books). If the word ends in ة, the ة opens up into ت first: خَالَة → خَالَتَانِ, غُرْفَة → غُرْفَتَانِ. That is the whole rule she was giving you.

THE SECOND ENDING, which is where it usually confuses people: ـَانِ is only for the DOER of the sentence. Everywhere else — after a preposition, or as the thing being acted on — it becomes ـَيْنِ. خَالَانِ فِي البَيْتِ (two uncles are in the house) but مَعَ خَالَيْنِ (with two uncles). Say them out loud — ‘-aan’ and ‘-ayn’ — and you will hear which one a sentence wants.

Anything describing a dual goes dual too: غُرْفَتَانِ كَبِيرَتَانِ, two big rooms. And a few words are almost always dual: وَالِدَانِ (parents), يَدَانِ (hands), عَيْنَانِ (eyes). From the class of 30 Aug.

examples.en: uncle → two uncles. Just add ـَانِ.
aunt → two aunts. The ة opens into ت first.
I have two uncles and two aunts. (hers, 30 Aug)
I went with two uncles — after مَعَ it must be ـَيْنِ, not ـَانِ.
In the flat there are two big rooms — the adjective goes dual as well.

test.prompt: Make “two aunts” from خَالَة (watch the ة)
‘I have two uncles and two aunts.’
‘with two uncles’ — careful, this one is not ـَانِ

patterns.name: يُوجَدُ — there is, there are
patterns.what: To say something exists somewhere, Arabic uses يُوجَدُ ('is found'), or just puts the place first with no verb at all: فِي المَطْبَخِ ثَلَّاجَةٌ — 'in the kitchen (is) a fridge'. There is no word for 'is'. The question form is the one she put on the board: مَاذَا يُوجَدُ فِي بَيْتِكَ؟

examples.ar: مَاذَا يُوجَدُ فِي بَيْتِكَ مِنَ الأَثَاثِ؟
examples.en: What furniture is there in your house?
In the kitchen there is a fridge and an oven.
There is no lift.

test.prompt: 'In the kitchen there is a fridge and an oven.'
'What is there in your house, of furniture?'
test.ar: مَاذَا يُوجَدُ فِي بَيْتِكَ مِنَ الأَثَاثِ؟
test.hint: maadhaa yuujadu fii baytika mina l-athaath

patterns.name: sentences with no verb at all
patterns.what: Arabic has no word for 'is'. To say 'the flat is beautiful' you just put the two words next to each other: الشَّقَّةُ جَمِيلَةٌ — literally 'the flat, beautiful'. The giveaway is that the first word has ال and the second does not: that gap is where the 'is' would be. الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ is the same shape — 'the praise, to Allah'. Half of everyday Arabic and a great deal of the Qur'an is built this way, so when you hear two nouns and no verb, put an 'is' between them.

examples.en: (All) praise is to Allah. (1:2)
Allah is One. (112:1)
The lamp is small.

patterns.name: the question words
patterns.what: Eight words open almost every question you will hear. هَلْ turns a statement into a yes/no question — هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ مِصْعَدٌ؟ 'do you have a lift?'. Then the ones that ask for information: مَا / مَاذَا what, مَنْ who, أَيْنَ where, مَتَى when, كَيْفَ how, كَمْ how many, لِمَاذَا why. They come first in the sentence, and the rest of it does not change order the way English's does. The Qur'an asks constantly — مَا الْقَارِعَةُ, and every أَلَمْ تَرَ is a question too.

examples.en: What is the Striking Calamity? (101:2)
Where is the Kaaba from here?
Do you have a lift?

patterns.name: plurals — and the rule nobody warns you about
patterns.what:
Three kinds. Sound masculine adds ـُونَ or ـِينَ: مُسْلِم → مُسْلِمُونَ. Sound feminine adds ـَات: مُعَلِّمَة → مُعَلِّمَات. And broken plurals rebuild the word from the inside — كِتَاب → كُتُب, بَيْت → بُيُوت, غُرْفَة → غُرَف. Broken ones have to be learnt with the word; there is no shortcut.

THE RULE THAT CATCHES EVERYONE: a plural of NON-HUMAN things is treated as feminine SINGULAR. Not الْكُتُبُ جُدُدٌ but الْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ — 'the books, she is new'. Same in the Qur'an: الْأَنْهَارُ تَجْرِي, the rivers 'she' flows. People take normal plural agreement; everything else does not.

examples.en: The cupboards are new — 'new' is feminine singular, because cupboards are not people.
Indeed those who believed and did righteous deeds (a sound feminine plural).
We have many sofas and chairs — again feminine singular.

patterns.name: telling someone to do something
patterns.what:
Take the present tense, cut the يَـ / تَـ off the front, and if what is left will not start a word, put an ا on the front to help: يَذْهَبُ → اذْهَبْ go!, يَقْرَأُ → اقْرَأْ read!, يَقُولُ → قُلْ say!. Speaking to more than one person, add ـُوا: اسْتَوُوا straighten up!, تَقَدَّمُوا move forward!.

You will hear this more than you say it. The Qur'an opens surahs with it — قُلْ, اقْرَأْ — and everything the imam says before prayer is in this form.

examples.en: Say: He is Allah, One. (112:1)
Read, in the name of your Lord. (96:1)
Straighten up and close the gaps! (what the imam says)

patterns.name: this and that
patterns.what:
هَذَا this (masculine), هَذِهِ this (feminine), ذَلِكَ that, تِلْكَ that (feminine). They must match what they point at: هَذَا زَوْجُ أُخْتِي but هَذِهِ الشَّقَّةُ.

One thing to watch: هَذَا الْبَيْتُ with ال on the noun means 'THIS house', while هَذَا بَيْتٌ without it means 'this IS a house'. The ال is doing the work of the missing verb, exactly as in the no-verb sentences.

examples.en: That is the Book, no doubt in it. (2:2)
This is my sister's husband.
Is this flat available?

patterns.name: كَانَ — the past tense of 'is'
patterns.what: Since Arabic has no 'is' in the present, it needs a word for 'was': كَانَ. كَانَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرًا — the house was big. Note the ending on the second word: after كَانَ the description takes -an (كَبِيرًا, غَفُورًا), which is the single clearest signal in the language that كَانَ is in play. Its negative is لَمْ يَكُنْ, and you already know it from Al-Ikhlas: لَمْ يَكُن لَّهُ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ.

examples.en: And there was none comparable to Him. (112:4)

examples.ar: كَانَ فِي غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ سَرِيرٌ وَمِرْآةٌ
examples.en: In the bedroom there was a bed and a mirror.
Allah was ever Forgiving, Merciful.

test.prompt: 'In the bedroom there was a bed.'
'there was none' — the phrase from Al-Ikhlas
